title: The Berlin Interpretation (IRDC 2008, mailing-list post)
label: practitioner
claim: Definition drafted by IRDC 2008 attendees, built on a canon of five games (ADOM, Angband, Crawl, NetHack, Rogue); stated purpose is community understanding, not constraining developers; missing a trait does not decide membership. High-value factors: random environment generation, permadeath, turn-based, grid-based, non-modal, complexity (several solutions via item/monster interactions), resource management, hack'n'slash, exploration and discovery (item identification redone every game). Low-value: single player character, monsters similar to players, tactical challenge, ASCII display, dungeons, numbers. Read through a summariser (WebFetch said it would not reproduce verbatim), so lists are paraphrase; the post's own counts differ from some secondary sources (8 vs 9 high-value). Community definition, not designer principles and not player data.

title: Soren Johnson, GD Column 17: Water Finds a Crack (Game Developer, March 2011)
label: developer
claim: Johnson (Civ III/IV) argues players treat games as optimisation problems and exploit any hole: 'Given the opportunity, players will optimize the fun out of a game.' Examples: Civ III forest lumberjacking, Civ infinite city sleaze (small-city spam beat large cities, trivialising high difficulties), Morrowind wall-running to raise skills, Ultima Online tank-mages. Fixes he reports: Civ IV per-city maintenance cost scaling with city count; overflow carried to next item; judge whether an exploit crowds out other styles or is a fun shortcut; give players a toggle (Civ III optional random seed against save-reload). Some exploits (Mario 1-up trick) he calls positive. Designer experience, no player data. Read via summariser.

title: Soren Johnson, Sid Meier's Key Design Lessons (Game Developer column)
label: developer
claim: Johnson relays Meier's rules from his years at Firaxis: 'a good game is a series of interesting choices' (Johnson adds choices matter only when informed); the player must 'always be the star' (in some simulation-heavy games 'either the designer or the computer was the one having the fun, not the player'); double it or cut it by half; 'one good game beats two great ones' (Covert Action: 'having two games competing with each other'); do research after the game is done ('the player shouldn't have to read the same books the designer has read'). Secondhand relay of Meier by his ex-colleague.

title: Leigh Alexander report on Sid Meier, Interesting Decisions (GDC 2012)
label: developer
claim: News report of Meier's talk, so quotes are the reporter's capture, not a transcript. Meier: games are a series of interesting decisions; good decisions are situational and can express play style; risk/reward and short vs long term recur across genres. Pitfalls: a dominant option (always picking the first) is a non-choice; rapid-fire complicated decisions make 'the player feel out of control'; simple decisions at slow moments bore; 'almost worth erring on the side of providing the player with too much information'; designers wrongly assume everyone plays like them; 'Be ruthless' cutting, a third or more of attempts removed; silence after a choice is bad ('The worst thing you can do is just move on'; even a sound effect). Another coverage piece (not fetched, search summary only) quotes 'something that's interesting you do once doesn't mean it's something interesting to do ten times'; and notes puzzle and rhythm games are the counterexamples critics raise.

title: Gigazine summary of Maddy Thorson's Celeste game-feel Twitter thread (March 2020)
label: developer
claim: Secondhand summary of Thorson's thread of ten assists, all widening timing or position windows in the player's favour: coyote time (jump briefly after leaving ledge; reason given: fewer fall deaths), jump buffering (jump pressed shortly before landing fires on landing frame; reason: quick repeated jumps), halved gravity at jump peak when jump held, jump corner correction (half step), dash corner correction, semi-solid platform pop-up, lift momentum kept 'a few frames', wall jump from 2 pixels away (at 320x180 'not small'), super wall jump from 5 pixels, stamina refund. Thorson: 'We add a little cheating to the operation to improve the player's feeling of operation.' No frame counts for coyote time or buffering in this source; a '5-frame' figure seen elsewhere came from an unverifiable site and is not recorded.

title: Roguelikes and narrative design with Hades creative director Greg Kasavin (GDC Podcast ep. 16 write-up, Jan 2021)
label: developer
claim: Written summary with excerpts, not full transcript. Kasavin: even resetting roguelikes leave the player something to carry forward, 'your knowledge of the mechanics' (Spelunky as example); asks 'you don't really die for real in roguelike games?' as a narrative hook; imagined a roguelike where 'every time you run into a boss, they remember'; story-engaged players hit by a difficulty wall is 'nothing more frustrating', so Supergiant built systems to let less experienced players work through. Does not state what players expect from the genre.

title: John Harris interview with Hempuli (Arvi Teikari), Game Developer, May 2019
label: developer
claim: Interview, not talk. Rule conflicts: 'Baba Is Not You' invalidates 'Baba Is You'; stacked words forced a rule-system rework. Areas are divided 'by words they introduce'; harder levels in an area 'nudge the player to look elsewhere'. Main limit: 'the levels very easily become overwhelming as the number of initially-active rules increases'. 'Extra' markers stop players tackling tough levels too early; level numbering 'works against this return-here-later design mindset'. Does not discuss tutorials or hints. Other secondhand mentions (search summary only, not fetched): rewind encourages experiment; Snakebird and Braid named as influences; he says one designer deciding everything can lose sight of difficulty.

title: Zachtronics approach to open-ended puzzle design (GDC 2019 talk page, Game Developer)
label: developer
claim: Page is only a talk blurb: Zachtronics often releases puzzles 'that the designers themselves haven't solved (or haven't optimally solved)' and trusts 'players will come up with their own unique solutions'. Talk is an interview of Zach Barth; I did not see transcript or slides. Infinifactory's worldwide histogram per criterion (search summary) is not confirmed as part of this talk.

title: Jon Blow on the truth in game design (GDC Europe 2011 talk report)
label: developer
claim: Report says Blow holds games are 'biased toward revealing truth, so long as we do not quash the truth in order to force our own high-level wishes into the design'; the system answers design questions, so the designer observes what emerges. Page says nothing on puzzle filler or specific puzzle rules. Not the ten Bosch/Blow IndieCade talk itself, which I could not obtain as text.

title: Marc ten Bosch blog, Designing to Reveal the Nature of the Universe (IndieCade 2011)
label: developer
claim: Blog blurb only. Talk favours 'a game design aesthetic that values looking for systems that express these truths in the cleanest possible way', examining how a system behaves and where its patterns lead, contrasted with 'more-traditional combinatoric design techniques'. No transcript retrieved; the video exists on YouTube per search summary but was not seen.

title: Derek Yu, Spelunky (Boss Fight Books) excerpt reprinted by Game Developer / GameDiscoverCo
label: developer
claim: Yu's own book text: 'In a game with randomized levels, people will keep playing just to see what comes up', but making it 'more than a glorified slot machine requires putting together a collection of systems and rules'; compares the RNG to Fate setting up scenarios that feel scripted. Does not address fairness or permadeath. Other Yu claims (random obstacles are solvable like any obstacle; hard choices with satisfaction and regret; players should blame themselves for death) seen only in search summaries, and the last from an unreliable fan site: not recorded as findings.

title: Henri Brouard, RimWorld, Dwarf Fortress and procedurally generated storytelling (Game Developer, 2019)
label: opinion
claim: Third-party article. Reports both games call themselves story generators; says Sylvester argues sparse visuals help players supply meaning (apophenia) and used a GDC talk example of a doctor about to operate on his wife. The article gives no verbatim quotes from Sylvester or Adams, so these are paraphrases of paraphrase.

title: Search snippet quoting Sylvester, Designing Games (2013): experience as arc of emotions
label: snippet
claim: Quote attributed to the book: 'An EXPERIENCE is an arc of emotions, thoughts, and decisions inside the player's mind.' Seen in a search result only. Search summaries, from fan blogs and a 2016 interview report, also say Sylvester argues games exist to generate experiences with the player ('if you just want to tell stories write a book'), that RimWorld uses AI storytellers (Cassandra, Phoebe, Randy; modelled on Left 4 Dead's AI Director per a German-language source). None verified against the book.

title: Giovannetti, Slay the Spire: Metrics Driven Design and Balance (GDC 2019) talk page
label: snippet
claim: Talk blurbs only: team relied on metrics from early development through Early Access, used player feedback on balance, and kept game feel and difficulty while patching frequently. No design principle stated on the pages. A design-analysis site's claim of per-card win and pick rates over millions of runs is unconfirmed and not recorded.

title: Sarian, 'No Going Back': The Telltale Model as Thought Experiment (Eludamos)
label: research
claim: Humanities argument, no player data. Telltale choices draw criticism since The Walking Dead (2012) for not mattering; author argues they work as a thought experiment, a sequence of moral dilemmas on one theme, and the final choice tests whether the player absorbed the theme rather than accumulating consequences.

title: Lewis, McGuire, Fox, Mapping the Mental Space of Game Genres (SIGGRAPH Sandbox 2007)
label: research
claim: Online survey of players' pairwise similarity judgments of games, analysed with manifold learning. Finds clusters that 'sometimes contradict current marketing genres' and concludes players 'primarily distinguish games not by traditional genres but instead by aesthetic and mechanics'. Sample size and game count not on the page. Closest direct evidence retrieved on genre as a player mental model.

title: Quantic Foundry coverage (search summary): 12 motivations, 1.75 million participants, strategy motivation declining
label: snippet
claim: Search summary says Quantic Foundry's 12-motivation model rests on over 1.75 million participants, that interest in strategic planning fell over nine years (67% now below the June 2015 average), and that Yee argues motivations predict enjoyment better than genre labels. No puzzle or roguelike figures found. Not opened.

title: Oliver and Pelletier (DiGRA 2005), already in genre-fit.jsonl; cited for the transfer-of-experience angle
label: research
claim: Carried from the existing evidence file, not re-read: qualitative Deus Ex study on how players transfer prior gaming experience; implication that games should recognise it. Added here only to avoid a duplicate search.
